newsitem.title: CHINA: Top China executive hits out at U.S. funding charge.
newsitem.headline: Top China executive hits out at U.S. funding charge.

text.p: The head of China's flagship international investment house and its main arms trader dismissed recent allegations that he paid to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton, the China Daily said on Monday.

Wang attended a February 1996 White House reception, a visit Clinton later said he regretted had occurred and which has fuelled suggestions of Chinese involvement in raising funds to the Democrats in the 1996 presidential campaign.
"No sensible men will be trapped by these malicious instigations," the newspaper quoted Wang Jun as saying.
Wang is chairman of the China International Trust and Investment Corp (CITIC) and is also head of major state weapons trader, China Poly Group.
Wang said he planned to respond to the allegations, including an article carried by The New York Times this month, but did not specify whether he planned to bring libel charges.

"I shall make a necessary response in due course since the article in The New York Times by William Safire has tarnished my good name," said Wang, son of China's late vice president Wang Zhen, a close associate of late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Wang dismissed the New York Times report that suggested Wang gave $50,000 to a middleman to arrange his meeting with Clinton, the China Daily said.

Wang said the article was aimed at damaging hard-won recent improvements in troubled Sino-U.S. ties that are set to culminate in October with a state visit by Chinese President Jiang Zemin to the United States.

"The libel represents an ulterior attempt by a tiny number of people, who try to make use of some anti-China force and mass media in the U.S. to create new barriers to disrupt the Sino-U.S. relationship," Wang said.

"What a gross irony it is to see in such a country as the United States, which claims to be the champion of democracy, someone can make up sensational lies in total disregard of facts and have them published in the press to sling mud at innocent people," Wang said.
A U.S. Senate committee investigating the funding scandal heard allegations earlier this month that Wang's ties to top officials made him a link to China's government in the scandal.
China has repeatedly denied that it made illegal donations to Clinton's 1996 election campaign.

Meanwhile a former restaurant owner in Little Rock, Arkansas, and a large contributor to the Democratic party said on Sunday he may be enticed to return to the United States from China as early as this week.
Charles Yah Lin Trie, in an interview with ABC-TV's "World News Tonight," said his lawyers had been urging him to come back and make a deal with the Justice Department.
Trie, who has been living in Beijing for the past few weeks, dismissed allegations that he engaged in espionage for the Chinese government as "totally...false".

Trie has refused to testify before the Senate committee investigating the campaign finance scandals. The Democratic National Committee has returned the $645,000 donated or raised by Trie from Asian-American sources.

The committee is investigating how foreign money was illegally raised and spent in the 1996 elections and whether U.S. security was compromised by individuals who may have shared secret information with foreign business interests.
